claims.title: Birdmen across two worlds
claims.dek: Birds, bent limbs and rounded forms, across a vast interval in place and time.
claims.anomaly: The recurring features invite a comparison between repertoires, rather than a single fortunate pairing. A historical link would have to bridge a very large chronology gap.
features: Both groups include bird imagery in complex carved or painted scenes.
The narrow bird-and-rounded-form correspondence is strongest for Pillar 43 and the Orongo boulder; it is not equally present in every group member.
differences: The Rapanui group includes human–bird hybrids; the Pillar 43 figure is generally described as a vulture.
The moai’s ring is below the birdmen; the boulder’s rounded object is at a bent hand; Pillar 43’s disc lies above a wing.
The group samples were selected for this inquiry. They do not establish how common or rare the combination is.

diffusion.note: No transmission sequence for this specific comparison has been established in the sources reviewed. That is not proof that contact was impossible.

origin.note: Starting comparison from the supplied project material; Lee Paqui’s 2024 article independently states the narrower bird-and-rounded-object parallel.

next_steps: Build dated local sequences on both sides.
Use expert-reviewed feature locations and relations before any similarity ranking.
Add a documented comparison corpus selected independently of the proposed match.

leads.title: San Agustín and Karahantepe · animal over a human back
leads.note: The two locations are the poster’s attributions. Object numbers, photo credits, dates and original contexts have not been verified here.
leads.next_step: Trace both sculptures to museum or excavation records; document the creature’s position and whether the human carries or wears it.

leads.title: Egypt, Mexico and a Māori-labelled drawing
leads.note: The two Mexican panels show the same Olmec monument, La Venta 19. “South America” and “Aztecs, Toltecs” mislabel it. The Egyptian “Hapi” and Māori attributions remain untraced. “Quetzalcoatl” is not a verified identification of the seated figure.
leads.next_step: Find the Egyptian object and original Māori illustration; retain the two Mexican views under one physical identity.

leads.title: Faces within birdlike masks
leads.note: Three views may include the same architectural carving. No site, period or collection identity has been adopted from resemblance alone.
leads.next_step: Match the architecture and carving to a site record before splitting these into separate objects.

leads.title: A lion-holder with a modern afterlife
leads.note: The left figure is Sydney’s modern Gilgamesh, unveiled in 2000. The right is an Assyrian hero type; its exact Louvre accession needs image matching. This is a useful modern reception control, not an independent ancient Australian parallel.
leads.next_step: Trace the modern artist’s sources and identify the particular Assyrian relief.

leads.title: The Egyptian-style ibis-headed figure
leads.note: The image resembles Thoth iconography. It has no object identifier or provenance; a modern reproduction remains possible.
leads.next_step: Find the original object or maker before assigning an ancient date.

leads.title: Another bird-headed protective relief
leads.note: Bucket, cone and bird-headed figure are visible. It is not assumed to be the Met panel already registered.
leads.next_step: Identify the museum relief and attach this image to its correct object.

leads.title: Modern feather regalia in a bird-costume argument
leads.note: The post proposes that bird figures represent costumed people. A modern performance photograph does not identify the meaning of an ancient carving; community and event are unverified.
leads.next_step: Trace the photograph and relevant community interpretation.

leads.title: Four Jiroft-labelled handled objects
leads.note: The screenshots extend the single Jiroft record with several designs. Their caption’s “3000 BC” is not an independently checked date; exact provenance and authenticity remain open.
leads.next_step: Match each design to an inventory and find context; establish whether any image repeats the existing record.

leads.title: Kimberley bark buckets and Pillar 43
leads.note: Fenton compares a bark bucket with the pillar’s upper forms. The ethnographic excerpt appears to concern Wunambal country in the Kimberley, not the Arnhem Land painting’s context.
leads.next_step: Verify the publication page and illustration, then record the container separately from the pillar’s uncertain interpretation.

leads.title: Body painting, tjurunga and pillar signs
leads.note: The archive traces the body-painting print to Wellcome 21428i; the pillar numbers and sacred-object collection remain untraced. The proposed relation is geometric, not a demonstrated common meaning.
leads.next_step: Consult the underlying collection records and appropriate community scholarship before coding the symbols.

leads.title: T-shaped headdresses and pillars
leads.note: Photographs resemble early Arrernte ceremony records, but the exact plates and rock painting remain unidentified. They are not evidence for a single Australian cultural unit.
leads.next_step: Identify the plates, communities and painting; compare outline separately from use.

leads.title: Yingarna, bags and creation
leads.note: The archive identifies the Injalak Hill painting and reports scholarship placing it among recent, post-contact paintings. It cannot be assigned the pillar’s Neolithic age.
leads.next_step: Follow the local interpretation and earliest documentation; separate the painting’s age from the age of the tradition.

leads.title: Lion Building graffito and Australian paintings
leads.note: The excavation description treats the squatting figure as a later graffito. Two Australian paintings remain unidentified; “birthing” is a proposed interpretation.
leads.next_step: Identify and date each depicted surface independently.

leads.title: Serpent heads, yam leaves and Rainbow Serpents
leads.note: One of four carvings is recognisable on Pillar 43; the other identities are unresolved. The yam-leaf analogy and shared-meaning proposal need separate tests.
leads.next_step: Identify the carvings, then compare literal head outlines against local snake and plant imagery.

leads.title: Serpent Mound and feathered-serpent imagery
leads.note: The thread compares a landscape monument with several creature images. The montage’s stone head and paintings remain unidentified; it is not a set of dated equivalent objects.
leads.next_step: Separate the mound, sculpture and paintings; obtain excavation and image sources for each.

leads.title: The “V-neck” comparison
leads.note: Fenton compares the Pillar 43 bird’s neck pattern with Urfa Man’s collar. The archive preserves the claim; the bird’s identity as a dressed human remains disputed.
leads.next_step: Compare the actual neck marks, local birds and local collars without assuming a shared garment.

leads.title: Animal images still to separate
leads.note: The architectural photograph and multi-object montage were in the atlas but absent from the catalogue. The montage cannot be coded wholesale as lizards or boars.
leads.next_step: Identify each distinct object and its original source; deduplicate repeat views.

leads.title: The circulating pillar–moai poster
leads.note: The moai image differs from the documented back. The supplied planning text calls it AI-generated, but its production history has not been proved. It is excluded as an archaeological photograph.
leads.next_step: Keep the poster as a presentation audit and compare only documented photographs.

leads.title: Cusco, Jerusalem and the name Göbekli Tepe
leads.note: The supplied planning note also mentions these centre/navel associations. No specific dated witness was supplied; the modern place name is not a Neolithic inscription.
leads.next_step: Trace each naming tradition to dated sources before adding cultural attestations.

leads.title: Other proposed rongorongo affinities
leads.note: The supplied AI research draft mentions Cuna/Guna pictographs, Chinese “Yü Pei” signs, Egyptian hieroglyphs, Shang oracle-bone signs, Sumatran ship-cloths, South American systems and Rapanui kai-kai. These are unverified bibliographic leads, not accepted identifications or explanations.
leads.next_step: Locate the original proposing publications; add specific signs and witnesses only after source checks.

leads.title: Local corpora and proposed comparison controls
leads.note: The planning note proposes Çatalhöyük, Nevalı Çori, Egyptian stelae, Izapa, Moche, Nazca, Northwest Coast crest art, Norse stones, Shang bronzes and Etowah plates, alongside already registered Assyrian, Australian and Cahokia material. These suggestions are not a completed corpus or evidence of independent invention.
leads.next_step: Select bounded, documented corpora before collecting similarity scores.
